movies.title: Daughters of the Dust
movies.why: Its patient attention to Gullah women makes ancestral memory the starting point of this collection.
lesson: Watch how the Peazant family weighs migration against connection to its island home. Memory is carried in bodies, objects, food and conversation, rather than supplied by a single authoritative narrator.

The film invites us to ask who gets to preserve a community's history. Its lyrical storytelling also challenges the expectation that every Black story must explain itself through familiar Hollywood conventions.

lesson: The three chapters follow Chiron as the pressures around him change the way he presents himself. Pay attention to the distance between a defensive exterior and an intimate moment of trust.

lesson: Katherine Johnson, Dorothy Vaughan and Mary Jackson confront institutions that undervalue their work. Watch the different forms of preparation, advocacy and cooperation each uses.

movies.title: The Burial of Kojo
movies.why: Its Ghanaian storytelling connects a child's perspective with dreamlike images and family history.
lesson: Esi remembers events through imagination, love and uncertainty. The film lets landscape and visual rhythm help tell a story that a plain explanation cannot contain.
Memory here is active rather than merely a record. Consider how a child makes meaning from adult events and how images can preserve emotional truth while remaining ambiguous.
movies.question: Can a dream reveal something a factual account misses?

movies.title: This Is Not a Burial, It's a Resurrection
movies.why: It centers an older woman's refusal to let a community's history be treated as disposable.
lesson: A proposed development threatens a village and its burial grounds. Mantoa's grief becomes connected to a struggle over land and collective memory.
The film questions who defines progress and who bears its cost. Notice how sound and landscape make belonging tangible beyond legal ownership.
movies.question: Who should decide what counts as progress?

movies.title: Neptune Frost
movies.why: Its experimental musical imagines resistance through technology, labor and identity.
lesson: A cyberpunk world connects extraction to the machines and networks people use. Songs and shifting identities make the film a sensory experience rather than a conventional explanation.
The story invites thought about the people behind digital convenience. Its imaginative form also questions who gets to design a future and whose labor disappears from that vision.
movies.question: Whose work makes technology possible?

movies.title: Saint Omer
movies.why: It asks viewers to examine judgment, motherhood and the limits of identification.
lesson: A writer attends a trial and finds the testimony unsettling her own assumptions. Long scenes of listening make uncertainty part of the experience.
The film resists turning a disturbing case into easy certainty. Consider how race, migration and personal memory affect the listener without assuming they explain every action.
movies.question: When does understanding require admitting uncertainty?

movies.title: Girlhood
movies.why: It gives Black French girls a vivid screen presence and a complicated search for autonomy.
lesson: Marieme finds friendship while negotiating constrained choices. Group identity offers pleasure and protection, but it also creates expectations.
The film's perspective invites discussion about both representation and authorship. Notice when shared joy opens possibilities and when fitting in narrows them.
movies.question: How can belonging both protect and limit a person?

movies.title: Pressure
movies.why: It brings Black British generational differences and employment barriers into view.
lesson: Tony's expectations differ from those of his parents and politically engaged brother. Everyday encounters reveal how belonging can be questioned even in the country where someone was born.
The film offers a specific portrait of its time rather than a universal migration story. Discuss how generations can share a racial identity while experiencing the same place differently.
movies.question: What changes between arriving in a country and growing up there?

movies.title: Babylon
movies.why: Its sound-system world joins artistic energy to a critical portrait of exclusion.
lesson: Blue's music and friendships exist alongside pressures from work and racism. Sound is a communal practice as well as an individual ambition.
The film's violence should be discussed through its consequences and context. Its strongest invitation is to hear a community's creative voice rather than reduce that community to danger.
movies.question: How can music create a place to belong?

movies.title: Burning an Illusion
movies.why: It treats a Black British woman's political and personal growth as a substantial story.
lesson: Pat's relationships and aspirations unfold amid the pressures of her society. Change comes through experience, disagreement and reconsideration.
The film complicates any assumption that political awakening follows a single script. Notice how everyday decisions become connected to larger questions about identity and power.

movies.title: The Stuart Hall Project
movies.why: It connects an influential thinker's public voice to migration, belonging and a changing Britain.
lesson: Archive and music assemble a portrait of Stuart Hall's evolving thought. The film lets historical events and personal experience shape intellectual questions.
A documentary portrait is selective even when its subject supplies much of the language. Ask how editing creates a relationship between a life and the ideas associated with it.

movies.title: Small Axe: Lovers Rock
movies.why: This standalone film values a party's atmosphere as a space of Black intimacy and collective joy.
lesson: One night is built from sound, movement and small negotiations between people. The film makes time spent together feel worthy of sustained attention.
Included as a standalone feature within the Small Axe anthology, it widens the idea of what an important story can be. Community pleasure is part of history, not merely an interval between hardships.

movies.title: Fruitvale Station
movies.why: It insists on Oscar Grant's personhood before the event that made his name widely known.
lesson: The film follows relationships, errands and ordinary efforts across a day. That attention challenges the reduction of a person to a headline or final image.
The narrative dramatizes a real life and contains painful material. Discussion should respect the people involved while distinguishing the film's reconstruction from verified documentation.
movies.question: What do ordinary details restore to a public story?

upcoming.title: Sinners
upcoming.why: Its musical imagination connects community ownership to a frightening struggle over who consumes Black culture.
lesson: The film brings blues, gathering and family into a supernatural conflict. Notice how musical performance becomes both a celebration and a point of vulnerability.
Its horror is fiction, while its setting invites historical study of racial exclusion and cultural exchange. Consider the difference between sharing an art form and losing the authority to shape it.
upcoming.question: Who should control the future of a community's culture?

upcoming.title: Sing Sing
upcoming.why: It recognizes creativity and collaboration as parts of personhood within incarceration.
lesson: A theater program offers a group of incarcerated men opportunities to perform, collaborate and imagine differently. The relationships matter as much as the production.

The story invites discussion of dignity without requiring that a person prove exceptional talent to deserve humane treatment. Explore the actual Rehabilitation Through the Arts program alongside the film.
upcoming.question: What can making art together change?

upcoming.title: Nickel Boys
upcoming.why: Its point-of-view filmmaking insists on seeing young Black people as subjects rather than distant objects.
lesson: Two boys form a connection within an abusive reform school. The film's approach to perspective changes what viewers can see and how they experience institutional power.
Adapted from Colson Whitehead's novel, it invites further study of the historical abuses that informed the fiction. Consider how a cinematic viewpoint can become an ethical choice.
upcoming.question: How does looking through a character's eyes change your understanding?

upcoming.title: The Piano Lesson
upcoming.why: It makes an inherited object the center of a debate about memory, ownership and a family's future.
lesson: Family members disagree about a piano carrying the record of their ancestors. The conflict asks whether preserving an object and building an economic future must pull in opposite directions.
Adapted from August Wilson, the film makes history emotionally present within a household. Consider how descendants can disagree without either person caring less about their inheritance.
upcoming.question: What makes an inherited object more than property?
